related_questions.question: What disqualifies you from unemployment in California?

text_blocks.snippet: In California, you can be disqualified from receiving unemployment benefits if you quit your job without "good cause," are fired for "misconduct," fail to meet work search requirements, or provide false information on your claim. Additionally, you must be physically able and available to work, and actively seeking suitable employment.
snippet_highlighted_words: quit your job without "good cause," are fired for "misconduct," fail to meet work search requirements, or provide false information on your claim

list.title: Voluntarily Quitting Without Good Cause:
list.snippet: Leaving a job without a compelling reason, as defined by California's unemployment laws, can lead to disqualification.

list.title: Being Fired for Misconduct:
list.snippet: Misconduct, such as violating company rules, theft, harassment, or insubordination, can disqualify you.

list.title: Failing to Meet Work Search Requirements:
list.snippet: You must be actively looking for work and able to accept suitable employment. This includes documenting your job search efforts.

list.title: Providing False Information:
list.snippet: Providing false or misleading information on your application or during the certification process can lead to disqualification and potential penalties.

list.title: Not Meeting Base Period Wage Requirements:
list.snippet: You must have earned a certain amount of wages during a specific base period (usually the past 12 to 18 months) to qualify for benefits.

list.title: Availability for Work:
list.snippet: You must be able and available to work, meaning you are not prevented by personal obligations, health issues, or other factors from accepting a suitable job.

list.title: Suitable Work:
list.snippet: You must be willing to accept suitable work, which is defined as work that is reasonably related to your skills and experience.

list.title: Failing to Certify Weekly:
list.snippet: You must certify your eligibility weekly, which includes reporting any earnings and job search activities.

list.title: EDD's Determination:
list.snippet: The California Employment Development Department (EDD) will determine if you are eligible for benefits based on the information you provide and the employer's response.

list.title: Right to Appeal:
list.snippet: If your claim is denied, you have the right to appeal the decision and have a hearing.

list.title: Consult with an Attorney:
list.snippet: If you have questions about your eligibility or have been denied benefits, consider consulting with an attorney specializing in unemployment law.
